A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MODNAS work and contain readable main text, equations, algorithms, figures, tables and appendices. Retained material can be reliably matched across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix J report original MODNAS and baseline experiments on NAS-Bench-201, OFA, HAT and HW-GPT-Bench.

after.justification: V3 retains these original experiments and reports additional CIFAR-100, comparator, diagnostic and GPT-L memory results.

M1.justification: The general four-component MODNAS procedure is retained. For the new memory/perplexity experiment, Appendix H.3.1 explicitly omits device-wise MGD and uses preference-weighted scalarization because memory is treated as device-independent. This is a limited procedural adaptation.

E1.justification: V3 adds CIFAR-100 evaluation on edgegpu and Pixel3 (Figures 17–18). The original image-classification, translation and language-modeling datasets remain. Object detection and dense prediction are discussed as prospective applications, without reported evaluation.

E2.justification: V3 adds MODNAS with MiLeNAS to the retained ReinMax/GDAS comparison (v2 Figure 13; v3 Figure 15). It also evaluates Zico-NSGA-II on OFA in Table 6. The existing comparator collections remain in the retained experiments.

E3.justification: V3 adds a 100-evaluation, four-times-budget baseline comparison alongside the retained 50-evaluation comparison. It also introduces GPT-L memory/perplexity evaluation with models up to 774M parameters, bfloat16 precision and context size 1024 (H.3.1). Original device splits, search budgets and 24-preference evaluation remain.

E4.justification: Beyond the existing sampler, update-scheme and device-count ablations, v3 adds device-embedding clustering, preference-to-solution alignment, training/validation loss trajectories and a larger-budget sensitivity comparison (Figures 12, 26–27). The sampler analysis also includes MiLeNAS. These substantially expand evidence about representation learning, optimization behavior and comparative robustness.

E5.justification: Both versions report means of three independent NAS-Bench-201 search runs and retain the existing error bars and bands. The new extended-budget comparison uses the same three-run practice. No new seed specification, confidence-interval procedure or significance testing is introduced.

E6.justification: Existing benchmark results are largely retained, while substantial new findings are added. CIFAR-100 MODNAS HV is 0.90 on edgegpu and 0.91 on Pixel3. Table 6 reports Zico-NSGA-II HV of 0.689/0.690 versus MODNAS 0.757/0.763 on v100_64/titan_rtx_64. Figure 27 shows some baselines approaching the global front more closely with four times the budget, and Figure 32 adds a competitive GPT-L memory/perplexity front. These are additional comparisons under their stated settings.

T1.justification: Appendix H.1.4 adds a short analytical argument relating random-search success probability to the required number of samples. Existing Pareto definitions, bilevel objectives, MGD mathematics and Frank-Wolfe solver are retained. No new MODNAS convergence theorem or proof is supplied.

C1.justification: The central claims remain single-search Pareto-front profiling, conditioning on hardware and preferences, zero-shot device transfer, and favorable efficiency and performance across CNN and Transformer spaces. The revised contribution wording emphasizes fast approximation without materially redefining this existing objective.

C2.justification: V3 adds explicit limitations concerning tuning, local optima and proxy mismatch in Section 5. Appendix I discusses implicit regularization, instability and unresolved bilevel MGD convergence. H.1.4 qualifies the efficiency interpretation by acknowledging stronger fronts from sufficiently funded baselines, while H.1.2 explains duplicate solutions and incomplete preference coverage.

D1.justification: V3 newly documents quantization of continuous preferences before embedding lookup (D.2), expands the Architect forward/backward computation walkthrough (A.2), and specifies precision and context length for the new GPT-L experiment. These mostly extend documentation; code-access disclosure and the existing implementation details are retained.

R1.justification: V3 adds references and discussion covering MiLeNAS, zero-cost proxies, NAS regularization and MGD/bilevel convergence. It also connects prospective applications to YOLOBench, AutoDeepLab and dense-prediction research. The established positioning against constrained hardware-aware NAS and earlier hypernetwork approaches remains.

P1.justification: Much of the original prose and section sequence remains. V3 makes localized language and terminology edits, updates affiliations and citation style, adds an appendix contents page and a gradient-computation walkthrough, moves broader impact into Section 5, and places extended related work at the appendix end.

P2.justification: V3 substantially expands visual explanation with an inference schematic, embedding-clustering plots, preference-alignment visualization, new diagnostic and benchmark plots, and Table 6. The sampler comparison is redrawn with MiLeNAS and a revised HV scale. Most earlier plots are retained and repositioned within the ICLR layout.

improvement.justification: Relative to v2's already broad empirical study, v3 adds useful targeted comparisons and diagnostics. The four-times-budget experiment and explicit optimization/proxy limitations make the performance interpretation more candid, while implementation explanations improve transparency. Most original scientific content remains, and limited protocol and uncertainty detail for some additions constrains the overall gain.
